findings.issue: Source: Jove rained 'that he might wash it sooner into the sea' (the rain washes the wall into the sea); candidate: 'so that the sea would wash the wall away sooner' changes the agent and mechanism.
findings.fix: While the son of Menoetius tended Eurypylus’s wound inside the tent, the Argives and Trojans went on fighting desperately. But the trench and the high wall above it were not going to hold the Trojans back much longer. The Achaeans had built the wall to protect their ships, and had dug the trench all around it to keep both the ships and the rich spoils they had taken safe. But they had never offered a great sacrifice to the gods. Because it was built without the immortals’ consent, it did not last. As long as Hector lived, Achilles kept up his anger, and Priam’s city stayed unsacked, the great wall of the Achaeans stood firm. Then the bravest of the Trojans died, and many of the Argives too, though some were still alive. In the tenth year the city was sacked, and the Argives sailed home to their own country. After that Poseidon and Apollo made a plan to destroy the wall. They turned the streams of all the rivers that run from Mount Ida to the sea onto it: the Rhesus, the Heptaporus, the Caresus, the Rhodius, the Grenicus, the Aesopus, and goodly Scamander, and the Simois, where many a shield and helmet had fallen and many a hero of the race of demigods had bitten the dust. Phoebus Apollo brought the mouths of all these rivers together and sent them flowing against the wall for nine days. Zeus rained the whole time, so that the wall would be washed into the sea sooner. Poseidon himself, trident in hand, looked over the work. He threw into the sea all the foundations of beams and stones that the Achaeans had laid with so much toil. He leveled everything along the mighty stream of the Hellespont, and when the wall was swept away he spread a great beach of sand over the place where it had stood. Then he turned the rivers back into their old channels.
